note: First deck: 60 street cards for November to February. Sights and sounds only; no card names a person of the cast or a living person. Seasonal claims: wedding season is closed mid-December to mid-January (Kharmas), so wedding cards list 11, 12, 2; Republic Day rehearsals are January. `names`: capitalised names in the cards that a reader has looked at and passed (monuments and the dead), so that the linter's warning speaks only of names nobody has read.

cards.text: Fog fills the road so thoroughly that the trunks of the avenue trees come out of it one at a time, dark, and are gone again. A car goes by with its headlights on, tapping its horn.
A sweeper in a faded orange vest drags a broom of bundled twigs along the gutter in long strokes, and the dry leaves of the avenue trees move ahead of it in a rattling heap.
Pansies, petunias and phlox fill the beds along the verandah in purple, white and yellow, each bed edged with a row of whitewashed bricks set at a slant.
Marigolds in orange and lemon yellow crowd the edge of the lawn, heavy-headed, with a few bees going from flower to flower in the sun.
Parakeets stream over the compound wall in loud green lines, hundreds of them, and drop all at once into the top of one tall tree, screaming until the light goes.
From somewhere beyond the trees a brass band plays a film tune, the drums carrying further than the horns, and the sound swells and fades as the procession moves.
Jets cross the rooftops in a low tearing roar, three in a line, bound for the ceremonial avenue, and the crows go up from every tree at once.
A rhesus monkey sits on the compound wall turning a guava in its hands, bites once, and drops the rest into the road.
A watchman at the gate of the next bungalow crouches over a small fire of dry leaves and twigs, a grey blanket round his shoulders and his hands held out to the smoke.
The setting sun is a flat orange disc that has lost its edge in the haze, and the far end of the road has gone the colour of weak milk.
A water tanker crawls along the road spraying a fine fan from its rear, and the grey pavement turns dark behind it and begins to pale again within minutes.
A handcart heaped with red carrots, cauliflowers and white radish in tidy pyramids is pushed slowly along the wall, its owner calling the names of the vegetables in a long singing note.
A peahen walks the top of the compound wall with great care, one foot set exactly before the other, then drops into the neighbouring garden.
The compound walls along the road are limewashed white with a black band at the foot, and every gate carries its number in black paint and a brass plate gone green at the corners.
A paper star lantern, lit from inside, hangs in the porch of a house across the road, and from the direction of a distant church comes faint singing.
Three girls in yellow scarves cross the road arm in arm, and above the wall a paper kite, also yellow, trails its tail against the sky.
Boys from the servants' quarters bat a tennis ball against the end wall of a lane, and each time it cracks off the wall the crows lift from the nearest tree.
Rain drums on the porch roof and pocks the lawn, the leaves of the avenue trees shine and drip, and a crow sits hunched and sodden on the gatepost.
In the fog the Bara Gumbad is a grey block with no edges, and walkers are heard on the gravel before they appear, one at a time, and are swallowed again.
Walkers in woollen caps and shawls circle the path at a brisk pace, one man in a cardigan swinging his arms in wide windmills, a puff of breath going up from each of them.
A ring of twenty or so men and women stands on the lawn near the tombs, laughing loudly with their hands raised, stopping together and starting again at a clap.
The blue glazed tiles that remain on the upper wall of the Shish Gumbad are brightest where the low sun reaches them, small patches of turquoise on dull grey stone.
A teacher counts a file of schoolchildren in sweaters across the Athpula bridge, two by two, and the last pair stops to look down at the water channel.
A couple in wedding clothes pose in the arches of Muhammad Shah's tomb, gold heavy on the woman's red lehenga, while an assistant holds a white reflector at arm's length and walkers wait to pass.
Gardeners squat in a row at a flower bed and pull weeds by hand, dropping them into flat baskets they push ahead of them, a hose lying uncoiled on the path beside them.
The dome of the Bara Gumbad is a pale shape without outline and the far trees dissolve into brown haze; some of the walkers wear cloth masks over their mouths.
A band of jungle babblers hops across the lawn in a noisy huddle, turning over dead leaves, each calling to the others in a harsh chatter.
Sikandar Lodi's tomb stands inside its own high walled garden, a plain octagon under a shallow dome, and the gravel inside the gate carries the neat lines of a rake.
Parakeets go in and out of the small niches high in the sandstone arches, bright green against the red, and the stone below them is streaked white.
A black kite sits on the rim of the marble dome with its wings half open to the sun, and a second sails past below it without a beat of its wings.
The long stone water channels of the garden run straight to the foot of the plinth, dry, with a drift of leaves along the bed.
The red sandstone of the upper walls turns nearly orange where the late sun strikes it, and the marble of the dome takes a pale pink.
A guard blows a whistle at a boy who has stepped onto the lawn beside the central walk, and the boy steps back to the path without looking round.
Rain darkens the red sandstone to a deep maroon and turns the marble of the dome grey, water streaming from the seams of the plinth steps.
Steel shutters go up one after another along the arcade, each with a clatter, and a boy sprinkles water on the pavement in front of a shop from a steel mug.
Painted signboards above the stairways to the upper floors advertise a dentist, a chartered accountant, a yoga studio and an architect, each in a different lettering.
A man roasts sweet potatoes on a bed of coals in a handcart at the edge of the car park, turning them with tongs, the skins blackened and splitting.
A parking attendant in a reflective vest blows his whistle and guides a car backward into a gap barely larger than the car, his flat palm moving a few centimetres at a time.
At a sweet shop a cook stirs a wide black pan of grated carrot, milk and sugar with a long flat spoon, scraping the bottom as the mixture thickens and darkens.
Delivery riders in matching jackets wait in a row by their motorbikes outside a café, looking at their phones, and one lashes a square bag to a rack with a bungee cord.
At dusk the strings of small bulbs over the lane come on, one bulb in each string failing to, and the pavement under them fills with people carrying paper shopping bags.
A fruit shop has stacked oranges, pomegranates and green guavas in careful pyramids, and an assistant rubs each one with a cloth in turn.
Stone footprints are set into the path at the length of a walking stride, leading across the garden toward a low stone column, with a few leaves lying on them undisturbed.
A line of schoolchildren in grey uniforms walks the path of stone footprints, stepping from one to the next, with a teacher at the back counting heads.
Sparrows work the gravel under the hedge, and the traffic of the road beyond the wall is a steady soft hiss behind the trees.
A sweeper with a short-handled broom works along the garden path, bent double, gathering the fallen leaves to the edge of the beds in a neat curved line.
From the courts comes the flat knock of a ball struck cleanly and a voice calling the score, and a trolley of balls stands against the net post.
Mist lies on the long lawn in front of the building, and a line of dark footprints in the dew crosses it from the gate to the courts.
Along the verandah of the club cane chairs stand in a row with their backs to the wall, and a bearer in white with a red sash carries a tray of tea past them.
In the library of the club, bound volumes of old magazines stand behind glass doors, and under green-shaded lamps two members read newspapers held on wooden rods.
On the board by the entrance, typed notices announce a lecture on groundwater in the Gangetic plain, a Hindustani vocal recital and a film on the railways of Bengal, each held by four coloured pins.
The pond in the garden is half covered with the round leaves of water lilies, and sparrows drink from the stone edge where the water has dropped.
The main building is of rough dark brick under deep concrete slabs, and the late sun picks out each course of the brick along the long wall.
Members and guests sit on the lawn in the sun in shawls and jackets, cups on small tables, and a murmur of Hindi and English carries across the grass.
Through the closed door of a seminar room comes the even voice of a speaker reading a paper aloud, and now and then the rustle of many pages turning.
Files tied in faded red tape lie stacked on the tops of steel almirahs, each bundle numbered in white paint, and a few have slipped and lean against the wall.
On a long bench outside a section door, men sit with plastic folders on their knees and rise one by one when a peon calls a name in a flat voice.
A peon in khaki carries a tray of tea glasses in a wire frame along the corridor, the glasses chiming softly, and clerks lean aside to let him through.
At midday clerks sit on the lawn in front of the building with their jackets folded under them and tiffin boxes open, eating in the weak sun.
From a room at the end of the corridor comes the quick uneven clatter of a typewriter, stopping now and then at the ring of its bell.
